newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Looming troubles with IMF cloud Kazakh economy.
newsitem.headline: Looming troubles with IMF cloud Kazakh economy.

text.p: Looming trouble with the International Monetary Fund clouded the end of an investment summit in oil-rich Kazakhstan on Friday that was aimed at attracting foreign capital to the former Soviet republic.
"The IMF is worried about our tax receipts," Akhmetzhan Yesimov, Kazakhstan's first deputy prime minister, told a news conference at the end of the summit in the capital Almaty.
Yesimov said the Fund was worried by a new law which planned to give tax breaks to companies which made investment in the republic's troubled industry a priority.
"But these privileges will not hurt the state budget's tax receipts," he said, adding that he was travelling to Washington later this month to explain the republic's position to the IMF.
An international financial source in Almaty said the new law threatened a $446 million Extended Fund Facility (EFF) agreed with the Fund last year.
"It's an extremely serious problem," the source said. "There has to be more transparency on tax concessions."

A clash with the fund could have serious consequences for the Central Asian state as it is poised to go to international money markets this year to help pay off a mountain of pension and wage arrears.
The suspension of the loan would also damage the Kazakhs' image of commitment to tough market economic reform -- they see themselves as ahead of their ex-Soviet neighbours.

On Friday the republic, a vast swathe of dry steppe and rugged mountains five times the size of France, published its lowest inflation figure since the start of reforms in 1992 -- 0.4 percent for May versus 0.8 percent in April.

President Nursultan Nazarbayev on Thursday boasted the republic was second only to Hungary in eastern Europe in terms of investment per capita for its 16.9 million population, with $6 billion in foreign direct investment since independence in 1991.

The government is pushing forward a fire sale of large state enterprises where stakes in oil and gas firms, telecoms and other plum assets are being sold for billions of dollars to help pay pension arrears which total 30 billion tenge ($400 million).

But foreign investors, already alarmed that a deal is not always a deal in Kazakhstan, are concerned that the government has not provided the transparency in tenders and contracts that it had promised.

"The most important thing is that there be a level playing field for all investors," said Richard Smith, vice-president of U.S. Citibank N.A.'s operations in Kazakhstan. "We would like to be judged in the same way that local banks are," he said.
Dulat Kuanyshev, director of the Kazakh government's state investment committee, told Reuters there was room for improvement in the country's investment climate.
"The most painful part of reform is the corruption and bureaucracy but we will fight this," Kuanyshev said.
